Just over a week ago I sat in the hospital with my daughter. Her little body was still adjusting to the large volumes of formula that were being pumped into her through her newly placed NG tube. Every time I nursed her she threw up. So I stopped letting her nurse. A week ago Sunday her stomach had calmed and they released us to go home.
I haven't nursed her since. For the first time in four years (since my son was born) I am not breastfeeding. I feel a freedom that I haven't felt in four years, but I also feel a sense of loss. A sense of grief. It is likely that I will never nurse another baby. That particular bonding and intimacy I experienced with my children while breastfeeding is over. And it ended suddenly and when I wasn't expecting it.
A week ago today my husband and I flew to Washington DC. On Tuesday we spent all day at the National Cancer Institute. Our plans to fly home Wednesday were uprooted when they decided to have Bryan go through surgery on Friday. They would remove three tumors and use the white blood cells they found in those tumors for a new treatment. He would be enrolled in a study that was getting remarkable results. Our hopes lifted.
Wednesday was a day of stress, a day filled with the sort of administrative tasks I have always hated. Phone calls to change flights and hotels quickly led into phone calls to schedule G tube surgery for my daughter. There were doctors, therapists, and insurance workers to talk to. But by the end of the day there was a plan. I felt productive.
Thursday meant more tests at NIH and quickly Friday was upon us. After Bryan was admitted for surgery the doctors came and filled our ears with discouraging news. Bryan had already had too much radiation to qualify for the study we had planned on pursuing. He could still get the TIL cell therapy, but could not get it combined with other treatment. He would have to pursue some other treatment at home first or wait for another new trial to open. After having a clear plan we were back to an enigmatic reality full of options. And we were discouraged.
As we flew back to Arizona I was reminded of this TED talk, as well as this one, which both talk about how having more options makes us less happy and about how choice is not always a good thing. I'm feeling the truth of that right now.
I want to have a lot of options when it comes to Bryan's treatment. I want to be informed and in control. I want us to be the one's making the decisions. But, I also don't. Today I feel the weight of all of these decisions anew. I feel the fear of not choosing the best option. I feel the uncertainty and all the variables of unknowns involved in these decisions.
Unable to clearly process through the maze in my head and the wall I have firmly built around my heart, I share facts and half developed feelings. But I still choose to show up. I choose to continue to share. Would you hold on with me as I struggle to be here in this space right now? content:Speaker assistant says: 1. Queenstown, New Zealand

The rugged Southern Alps are perfect for hiking and snow sports. Its breathtaking scenery and charming town make it a must-visit destination for adventurous couples.

2. Banff, Canada
Banff is a picturesque mountain town nestled in the heart of the Canadian Rockies. It is a popular destination for skiing, hiking, and kayaking. The famous turquoise-colored Lake Louise is a must-see attraction, and the hot springs offer a relaxing après-adventure experience.

3. Patagonia, Argentina/Chile
Patagonia is one of the world's most breathtaking natural wonders, with rugged glaciers, towering mountains, and clear blue lakes. It is a true paradise for hikers and adventurers, with the famous Torres Del Paine National Park being a must-visit attraction.

4. Costa Rica
Costa Rica's natural beauty and eco-tourism make it a perfect destination for adventurous couples. With rainforests, volcanoes, and incredible wildlife, the country offers a variety of outdoor activities like zip-lining, surfing, and rafting. Couples can also relax in natural hot springs or visit the stunning waterfalls.

5. Iceland
Iceland is known for its otherworldly beauty, with rugged volcanoes, glaciers, and geysers. It is the perfect destination for couples seeking rugged landscapes and natural wonders like the Northern Lights, hot springs, and stunning waterfalls. Hiking, horseback riding, and glacier tours are beloved attractions.

6. Namibia
Namibia's wild and dramatic landscapes create an amazing environment for adventurous couples. It is best known for its stunning sand dunes, wildlife reserves, and national parks, leading to incredible safaris and animal sightings.

7. Alaska, USA
Alaska is the ultimate destination for outdoor enthusiasts seeking adventure in the wilderness. The state's unique wildlife and rugged natural beauty make it perfect for hiking, kayaking, and fishing. Whale watching and bear sightings are also among the beloved activities that couples can partake in.

8. Peru
Peru is a country rich in history, culture, and adventure. Hiking the famous Inca Trail to the ancient city of Machu Picchu is a bucket-list item for many couples. The country also boasts a variety of other outdoor activities like surfing, sandboarding, and white water rafting.

9. Bhutan
Bhutan is a completely unique destination, offering a blend of adventure and spirituality. Hiking and trekking are popular activities, with the beautiful Himalayas as a backdrop. The country is known for its beautiful landscapes, stunning architecture, and distinct culture.

10. Kalahari Desert, Botswana
The Kalahari Desert offers an unforgettable scenery and wildlife experience with rugged landscapes and fascinating animal sightings. Couples can enjoy activities like horseback riding, quad-biking, and stargazing. content:Speaker assistant says: The Industrial Revolution had a significant impact on British literature. It was a period of great change, and writers were inspired to use their works to explore and comment on these changes.

One of the most significant effects of the Industrial Revolution on literature was the rise of the novel. As people were becoming more literate and books were becoming more affordable, novels began to gain popularity. Writers like Charles Dickens, Elizabeth Gaskell, and Thomas Hardy wrote about the social and economic changes taking place in their society. Their novels often featured characters struggling with poverty, inequality, and the challenges of industrialization.

The Industrial Revolution also had an impact on poetry. The Romantic poets, like William Wordsworth, Samuel Taylor Coleridge, and John Keats, were inspired by the beauty of nature and their love for the natural world. However, as industrialization brought about changes to the landscape, they also began to write about the destruction of the natural world and the alienation of individuals in urban settings.

Overall, the Industrial Revolution had a complex impact on British literature. content:Speaker assistant says: British colonialism during the 16th to 19th century was primarily motivated by economic interests. The British sought colonies that would provide them with precious metals, raw materials, and convenient markets to sell their manufactured products. Trade was the most influential motivation for colonization, as it meant profit for merchants and the enrichment of the Crown's treasures. The goal of British colonialism was self-sufficiency or economic independence, and colonies were seen as a means to achieve this.

Initially, the British Empire consisted of scattered possessions such as Jamaica, Bahamas, Bengal, Gibraltar, and Bermuda, which were conquered in wars with France and Spain. The principal part of the first British Empire was formed by North American colonies stretching from the East coast to the Caribbean. During the Seven Years War, France lost all its Canadian possessions to Britain, which left the latter strong indebted, and therefore, the tax rate was increased. This led to the colonists protesting the taxation without representation, and the Boston Tea Party followed. The US independence resulted in the disruption of the first British Empire.

During the Victorian era, existing colonial possessions in Canada, the West Indies, and India were enlarged to import cotton, spice, tea, and the export of cloth and cotton goods. Colonies were primarily markets for British goods, and as a result, the policy of imperialism developed. Britain enlarged its empire within a century to such an extent that it became the largest colonial empire in history, comprising nearly one-fifth of the land surface.

However, as the colonies grew in size and prosperity, demands for self-government and sovereignty grew, leading to dissatisfaction with British rule and reforms and the rise of nationalism. - Natural resource distribution: Many Third World countries have an abundance of natural resources but are rich in non-renewable resources like oil, but are often poorly managed by the local governments.

Political Features:
- Authoritarian or autocratic regimes: Third World countries may have one-party systems or military rule, which can be brutal and suppressive of human rights.
- Civil unrest: Third World countries may have political instability that leads to civil wars, coups, and government overthrows.
- Disrespect of human rights: Third World countries may violate basic human rights like freedom of assembly, freedom of the press, and freedom of speech.
- Corruption: Corruption is prevalent in many Third World countries, and it can lead to financial instability and lack of economic growth.
- Lack of infrastructure: Many Third World countries lack the appropriate infrastructure needed to support their economies, such as transportation systems and healthcare facilities.

Social Features:
- Overpopulation: Third World countries tend to have larger populations with limited resources, leading to overpopulation in some areas.
- High poverty rates: Third World countries have a high poverty rate, with many people living on less than a dollar a day.
- Lack of access to education and basic needs: Third World countries may have limited access to basic needs like clean water, sanitary facilities, and education.
- Low life expectancy: Due to a lack of adequate healthcare facilities and living conditions, life expectancies tend to be lower in Third World countries.
- Widespread disease and epidemics: Malaria, HIV/AIDS, and other communicable diseases are often widespread in Third World countries.
- Poor housing conditions: There are many slum areas in Third World countries, which tend to have poor living conditions.

Economic Features:
- Lack of raw materials or natural resources: Some Third World countries have an inadequate amount of resources to support their economies.
- Low prices for exported goods: Many Third World countries sell their raw materials at low prices to industrialized countries that then process them into finished products and sell them at high prices.
